items.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Common-law courts have always preferred bright-line rules to flexible standards.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Modern federal procedure has eliminated all procedural barriers facing pro se litigants.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The drafters of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure rejected the influence of the common-law tradition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Twombly and Iqbal returned the federal courts to nineteenth-century pleading standards.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The shift from rigid pleading to notice pleading reflected a deliberate trade of doctrinal predictability for procedural access.

items.explanation: The passage's central thesis is that the move to notice pleading was a *trade-off*: the drafters knowingly sacrificed some predictability to widen the courthouse door. E captures both halves. A overstates ('always'). B is contradicted by the closing paragraph. C is too strong — the passage says drafters were *informed by* the tradition, not that they rejected it. D confuses the post-Iqbal tightening with a full reversion.

items.stem: The author's attitude toward Twombly and Iqbal is best described as one of…

choices.label: A
choices.text: uncritical endorsement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: open hostility.

choices.label: C
choices.text: qualified concern.

choices.label: D
choices.text: indifference.

choices.label: E
choices.text: scholarly bewilderment.

items.explanation: The author concedes that the cases addressed real problems (mass-tort fishing expeditions) but worries they 'risk reintroducing the very access barrier the 1938 drafters set out to dismantle.' That hedged worry is qualified concern (C), not endorsement, hostility, indifference, or bewilderment.

items.stem: According to the passage, the original Federal Rules of Civil Procedure took effect in…
items.explanation: Detail question. The passage states that 'the original Federal Rules of Civil Procedure … took effect in 1938.' 1957 is the year of Conley v. Gibson; the other dates appear nowhere as the adoption year.

items.stem: The author mentions the Field Code of 1848 primarily in order to…

choices.label: A
choices.text: argue that fact pleading was superior to the notice pleading that followed it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate an early reform effort that solved some problems but introduced new ones.

choices.label: C
choices.text: show that New York courts led all other jurisdictions in procedural innovation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that the writ system was never genuinely abandoned.

choices.label: E
choices.text: establish that procedural reform inevitably fails.

items.explanation: The Field Code is introduced as a 'partial remedy' to the writ system, but the next paragraph explains that 'fact pleading … generated its own pathologies.' B captures that role — an early reform that helped yet created new problems. A and E overstate the point; C and D assert claims the passage never makes.

items.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that defenders of Twombly and Iqbal believe that…

choices.label: A
choices.text: notice pleading should be abolished entirely.

choices.label: B
choices.text: pro se litigants rarely file meritorious claims.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Conley v. Gibson was wrongly decided from the outset.

choices.label: D
choices.text: changes in litigation since 1938 justify a more demanding pleading standard.

choices.label: E
choices.text: the Field Code offered a better model than the Federal Rules.

items.explanation: Defenders 'note that mass-tort and antitrust complaints had created discovery abuses the 1938 drafters could not have foreseen' — i.e., new litigation conditions warrant a tougher standard, which is D. A, B, C, and E go well beyond anything the defenders are said to claim.

items.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Privity of contract was an indefensible doctrine that nineteenth-century courts should have abandoned far sooner than they did.

choices.label: B
choices.text: American products-liability law moved from a privity bar through negligence to strict liability, yet strict liability retains substantial elements of negligence reasoning.

choices.label: C
choices.text: MacPherson v. Buick eliminated the requirement that an injured consumer prove a manufacturer's negligence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Restatement (Second) of Torts settled the long-running dispute over the proper basis of manufacturer liability.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Justice Traynor's concurrence in Escola was the most influential single opinion in the history of American tort law.

items.explanation: The passage traces an arc — privity bar, then negligence after MacPherson, then strict liability — and closes by stressing that strict liability still 'sits uneasily' with negligence reasoning. B captures both the arc and that tension. A states an evaluative claim the author never makes. C is false: the passage says MacPherson 'did not abolish the need to prove fault.' D is contradicted by the final paragraph, which says the question is still 'debatable.' E overstates a detail and is not the passage's overall point.

items.stem: According to the passage, the doctrine of privity of contract was crystallized in which one of the following cases?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Winterbottom v. Wright.

choices.label: B
choices.text: MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Escola v. Coca-Cola Bottling Co.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Greenman v. Yuba Power Products.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Conley v. Gibson.

items.explanation: Detail question. The first paragraph states that privity of contract was 'crystallized in the English case Winterbottom v. Wright (1842).' MacPherson (B) cracked the privity rule; Escola (C) and Greenman (D) belong to the strict-liability story; Conley v. Gibson (E) is a civil-procedure case that does not appear in this passage at all.

items.stem: The author refers to Justice Traynor's concurrence in Escola primarily in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: demonstrate that strict liability had already become the governing rule by 1944.

choices.label: B
choices.text: identify an early judicial argument for strict liability that courts would adopt only later.

choices.label: C
choices.text: criticize the Escola majority for reasoning that was internally inconsistent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: show that Cardozo's approach in MacPherson had been formally overruled.

choices.label: E
choices.text: establish that risk distribution is an inadequate justification for liability.

items.explanation: The passage presents the 1944 concurrence as urging a change that 'prevailed a generation later' in Greenman (1963) and §402A (1965) — i.e., an early argument adopted only afterward, which is B. A misreads the timeline (it was a concurrence, not the governing rule). C and D describe moves the author never makes. E states a critique the author raises only as one side of a 'debatable' question, not the reason for citing Traynor.

items.stem: The author's attitude toward describing modern products-liability law as 'strict' is best characterized as one of

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic agreement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: measured skepticism.

choices.label: C
choices.text: outright rejection of strict liability as a concept.

choices.label: D
choices.text: indifference to how the doctrine is labeled.

choices.label: E
choices.text: nostalgia for the privity requirement.

items.explanation: In the final paragraph the author concedes strict liability's risk-distribution rationale but warns that the 'strict-liability label can obscure how much negligence reasoning survives within it' — a hedged, doubting stance toward the label, i.e., measured skepticism (B). A is too positive. C overstates: the author questions the label, not the doctrine's existence. D is wrong because the author plainly cares about the label's accuracy. E finds no support; the author calls privity a remedyless 'price' borne by consumers.
